sources.title: Wang Yangming (Q378462), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Wang Yangming', English description 'Chinese philosopher and general (1472-1529)', Korean label '왕양명', born 1472-10-31, died 1529-01-09, citizen of Ming-era China. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Bryan Van Norden, 'Wang Yangming', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (first published 2014, substantive revision 17 September 2024), read in full via a page summary: his training in Zhu Xi's commentaries, the bamboo episode, the 1508 awakening in Guizhou, the disciples' compilation of the Record for Practice, the doctrines of the unity of knowing and acting, his rejection of Zhu Xi's reading of 'investigating things', his influence in Japan and in the School of Mind, and the criticisms of the Qing evidential-research scholars (Dai Zhen) and of modern philosophers. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (Britannica returned HTTP 403; the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy page returned 404). A scholarly reference entry by a named philosopher; it also records the critics.

Frederick Goodrich Henke (translator), 'The Philosophy of Wang Yang-ming' (Open Court Publishing Company, Chicago and London, 1916; Internet Archive full text), read in part: the translated chronological 'Biography of Wang Yang-ming' compiled by his Chinese followers (the Longchang episode, the teaching episodes, the disciples' gatherings, the objections raised to his teaching), the Record for Practice passage in which he says he did not discuss innate knowing until after Longchang, and his 'Instructions for His Disciples at Lungch'ang'. A disciples' record and his own writings: self-report and admiring; it contains legendary episodes that are not scored.

Miaw-fen Lu, 'The Construction and Development of the Yang-ming School' (in Chinese), Tsing Hua Journal of Chinese Studies 29(2), June 1999, pp. 167-203, abstract read on the journal's page (full text not opened): argues that the school was established in Wang's lifetime around him as a charismatic leader, that it met academic challenge and official persecution, that after his death the lecture assemblies of local gentry and students gave it diverse forms, and that its claim to autonomy from political power should not be overstated. An independent modern historian's account of the movement he founded.

Lin Zhan, 'Luo Qinshun (1465-1547) and His Fellow Scholars' Criticism of Wang Yangming's Learning and Its Contemporary Implications', PhD thesis, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (cover dated 2020, abstract dated July 2019), abstract and front matter read (the truncated copy did not include the chapters): reconstructs the critics of his learning in the Zhengde and Jiajing reigns, says his book on Zhu Xi's late conclusions is marred by numerous mistaken datings of Zhu Xi's writings and was written to maintain his disciples' confidence rather than for careful scholarship, and argues that the critics' scattered efforts left little lasting effect. A modern scholarly counter-voice; abstract only, so row confidence is capped.

Guizhou provincial government English-language news site, article on the 2023 book 'The Birth of Yangmingism' (updated 24 February 2023), read: says he was enlightened at Longchang in Xiuwen county in spring 1508 and in his second year in Guizhou lectured on the unity of inner knowledge and outer action at the Wenming Academy in Guiyang. A provincial government outlet promoting the region's Yangming heritage: promotional, used only to corroborate the Guizhou lecturing; no row rests on it alone.

Shanghai Museum, item page 'Ming, Cai Shixin, hanging-scroll portrait of Wang Yangming' (Chinese), read together with the museum's website copyright statement: item data (paper, colours, 106.2 x 33.7 cm, inscribed 'Portrait of Mr. Yangming', Ming dynasty) and the statement that website content is, unless otherwise noted, the museum's copyright, may not be used commercially without written permission and may not be modified. Used only for the portrait decision, not as support for any trait row.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_wangy_sep, src_wangy_henke, src_wangy_linzhan | 1499-1529 | philosophy reference entry + disciples' record + critics' thesis] Trained in the Zhu Xi curriculum that the examinations rested on, he came to reject Zhu Xi's reading of investigating things and became a leading critic of the orthodox view, founding with Lu Xiangshan the rival School of Mind (SEP); his critics in the Zhengde and Jiajing reigns organised against his teaching (Lin Zhan). The Qing scholar Dai Zhen is reported to have argued that his approach let subjective opinion pass as infallible moral sense, so the trait is recorded as dual-edged. Pre-modern, sparse record; his political and military career is not scored.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_wangy_sep, src_wangy_henke | 1489-1508 | philosophy reference entry + disciples' record] After the bamboo episode left him doubting Zhu Xi's method, he moved between Daoist, Buddhist and Confucian practice for years, and in 1508 concluded that moral truth lies in the mind and not in outside things (SEP); the disciples' record quotes him as saying he had been wrong to look for principles in things, and as dropping his Daoist exercises as 'not in accordance with the true way'. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.50 because the Daoist-exercise episode and the 'I was wrong' wording come only from the disciples' compiled biography, which also contains legendary episodes, and the independent reference entry corroborates only the general arc.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_wangy_henke, src_wangy_sep | 1489-1529 | disciples' record + own instructions + reference entry] The aim of becoming a sage organised his study from the bamboo episode through the Daoist and Buddhist years, and his instructions to his students at Longchang urge them to fix their determination, study diligently, correct errors and accept rebuke (self-authored). The pursuit is documented, but how persistently and with what method rests largely on self-report and a disciples' record.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_wangy_henke, src_wangy_lu1999, src_wangy_guizhou | 1509-1529 | disciples' record + modern historian + provincial government outlet] The disciples' record describes students gathering around him in the hundreds at Chuzhou and more than a hundred disciples at a gathering at home, and Lu argues the school was founded in his lifetime around him as a charismatic leader; a Guizhou outlet says he lectured at the Guiyang academy in his second year there. Lu also says his political and military success in Jiangxi was a turning point for the school, which confounds how much of the following was due to teaching alone, so the score is kept moderate.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_wangy_linzhan, src_wangy_sep | 1514-1515 | critics' thesis abstract + reference entry] Lin Zhan's abstract says his book on Zhu Xi's late conclusions is marred by numerous mistaken datings of Zhu Xi's writings and was written to maintain his disciples' confidence rather than for careful scholarship; the reference entry also raises objections to some of his arguments. This reads one work from an abstract only, so it is a limited, low-confidence reading and says nothing about the rest of his philosophical writing.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait resolved. (1) Wikidata's image is a crop of the Ming hanging-scroll portrait by Cai Shixin in the Shanghai Museum. The painting is public domain by age, but the digital image comes from the museum's website, whose copyright statement says website content is the museum's copyright, may not be used commercially without written permission and may not be modified; the museum offers no item-level open-access statement and our use would crop and downscale it. (2) A woodcut from the 1743 illustrated-biography book Wanxiaotang huazhuan by Shangguan Zhou (creator died long ago, so public domain by age) exists on Commons as 'Wang Shoujen.jpg', but the sitter is named only in the uploader's description and in a Wikipedia gallery table, no printed caption or scanned page of the book was found to confirm the sitter, and the Commons page cites a 1921 edition. (3) The 1916 frontispiece of Henke's translation is a photograph of a temple statue, a derivative work, so rejected; other Commons images have unknown authors or no source. Next step: either obtain written permission or an open-access item-level statement from the Shanghai Museum, or find a scan of the Wanxiaotang huazhuan page showing the printed caption 'Wang Shouren' and use that woodcut (historical depiction).
